title: Without the Guru
hookLine: line after line, the Sidh Gosht says what is missed without the True Guru

lines: A STRIPE OF PAINT ON A TREE.
cards: On a mountain trail, what matters can be tiny: a stripe of paint on a tree, a little pile of stones at a fork. Someone walked this way before you and left a sign.
Without it, the trail splits, the light goes, and every path looks the same. The yogis in the Sidh Gosht had their own teachers.
Near the poem's end, Nanak speaks to exactly that, in lines that each begin the same way: without the True Guru.

teach.h: WITHOUT THE TRUE GURU: NO WAY.
teach.b: Here are those lines, in paraphrase. Without serving the True Guru, there is no real yoga. Without meeting the True Guru, no one is set free.
Without meeting the True Guru, the Name can't be found. Without the True Guru, a person suffers deeply, lost in the dark of pride. And without the Guru, Nanak says, a person loses the game of life.
The repetition is the point, like someone tapping the same spot on the map: here, here, here. The yogis already had teachers, so the surprise isn't that a guide is needed.

teach.h: IN THIS POEM, THE GURU IS THE WORD.
teach.b: It's what this poem has said the Guru is. Two days ago, asked who his guru was, Nanak answered: the Word is the Guru, and attention tuned to it is the disciple.

So, read inside the Sidh Gosht, without the Guru means without that Word to steer by. Sikhs honor the ten Gurus and the Guru Granth Sahib as the Guru, the one light carrying that Word. And look how the week has built.
Why leave home? To seek the Gurmukhs. The earrings?
The Word, worn within. Where it all began? In wonder.
Where the mind lives? The Word steadies it. Who his guru was?
The Word. How to cross the ocean? Attention on the Word.
Every answer has pointed the same way, and today's lines say plainly why.
In this poem, nobody finds that way alone. The stripe of paint on the tree isn't an insult to the hiker. It's a gift from someone who went first.

how: Sikhs speak of the need for the Guru, the ten Gurus and the Guru Granth Sahib, as the guide to the Name, and the Sidh Gosht's lines on life without the True Guru are sung and explained in kirtan and katha.

o: Nanak's lines: without the True Guru, no yoga, no freedom, no Name
a warning that anyone without a teacher will be punished
a hymn of mourning for a Guru who has passed away

games.q: without the True Guru — tap the pairs.
p: can't be found without the Guru

s: the Sidh Gosht says a person can find the way alone
near its end it says, line after line, that without the True Guru the way isn't found.
in this poem, Nanak has already named the Word as the Guru
sabad guroo: the Word is the Guru, attention the disciple.
the repeated lines tell the yogis guides don't matter
they say a guide is needed, and name the True Guru as that guide.

games.q: you're a yogi who believes in teachers. near the end of the talk, Nanak returns to guides. what does he say?
o: that the wise need no guide at all.
that without the True Guru, no one is set free.
games.why: line after line: without the True Guru, no yoga, no freedom, no Name; and in this poem, the Guru is the Word.

practice: Let someone come to mind who showed you the way at a fork in your life, a teacher, a grandparent, a friend, an author, a stranger who said one right thing at the right time, and stay with their face, or the page, or the moment, for a few breaths.
Notice where you might be without that stripe of paint, and silently thank them. If you pray, say Waheguru on each slow breath, in thanks for every guide.

wordCard.voice: Without the Guru. The Sidh Gosht's run of lines near its end: without the True Guru, no yoga, no freedom, no Name. Today's word.

orig.note: satgur: the True Guru, named in each of the lines near the poem's end.

carryVoice: Your line: a guide is needed. In this poem, the guide is the Word. A week on the mountain, done.
